passage: A familiar story about civic life holds that ordinary people have withdrawn from it. Where their grandparents joined lodges, unions, parents' associations and choral societies, attended meetings and stood for office in them, people today are said to stay at home, absorbed in private amusements and too busy or too distrustful to join anything. The story is usually told as a matter of individual choice and individual failing, and the remedies proposed follow naturally from it: people should be encouraged, shamed or gently nudged back into joining.

There is another way to read much of the same evidence. What has declined is not association as such but a particular form of it: the federation of local branches, each with its own officers, meetings and dues, linked through elected delegates to regional and national bodies. In its place, many of the organisations that now claim to speak for citizens are run by professional staff from a central office. They recruit supporters through mailing lists and advertisements, ask them for money rather than time, and consult them, if at all, through surveys. Their membership lists may be long, but a member is someone who has made a payment, not someone who has attended a meeting, and nothing in the organisation's routine requires that members ever meet one another.

Read this way, the decline is less a withdrawal from below than a transformation from above. Organisations discovered that it was cheaper and more effective, at least for the purposes of lobbying and publicity, to raise money from many distant supporters than to sustain an expensive structure of local branches with their own halls, officers and opinions. Funders, too, preferred bodies with a clear national voice and a small, accountable staff, and the habits of professional management spread from one organisation to the next. The people who drifted away from the older associations may not have rejected participation at all; they may simply have been offered fewer occasions for it.

The distinction matters because the federated association did something its successors do not. It taught people with no political ambitions how to run a meeting, keep minutes, manage a budget, argue for a motion and accept defeat when it was voted down. These were not trivial accomplishments; they were the ordinary apprenticeship of democratic citizenship for many who would never hold public office. It also tied the local to the national: a member in a small town could, through a chain of elected representatives, influence what the national body did. A donor to a professionally managed organisation may support its aims with real conviction, but she learns none of these skills and holds no comparable thread of influence over what is done in her name.

It would be easy to turn this into nostalgia, and nostalgia would mislead. Many of the old associations excluded women or people of the wrong background, and their local meetings could be stifling and petty. The new organisations, for their part, have often been more effective at changing laws. Nor have people stopped gathering; they form online groups and informal networks with remarkable ease. But these are seldom built to govern themselves through elected officers and binding votes. If the loss is real, it is the loss of a school of self-government, and it will not be repaired by urging individuals to join more. It would require organisations to find reasons, and funders to give them reasons, to want members who turn up.

passage: Governments that once judged their success almost entirely by output have lately begun to ask citizens a different question: all things considered, how satisfied are you with your life these days? The answers, usually given on a scale from zero to ten, are collected, averaged and compared across regions and years, and a rising average is increasingly cited as evidence that policy is working. The appeal of this approach is easy to understand. Income is at best a means to living well, and a measure that asks people directly about their lives seems to cut out the middleman.

Yet the question is less direct than it looks. To answer it, a respondent must do something quite unlike reporting a sensation. She must call to mind her life as a whole, choose the standards by which it is to be judged, and compare the one with the other. The number she gives is therefore an evaluation, and evaluations depend on the standards brought to them. Two people whose days contain the same mixture of pleasure, worry and boredom may give very different scores because one expects more from life than the other. A person who has learned to expect little can report contentment with circumstances that would dismay a neighbour, and a population whose expectations rise quickly can report falling satisfaction even as its conditions improve.

None of this makes the surveys worthless. Evaluations matter in their own right: how people judge their lives shapes what they choose, whom they blame and whether they think change is possible. The scores also move in ways we would expect, dropping when people lose their jobs or fall seriously ill. The error lies not in collecting the numbers but in treating them as a complete reading of how well people are living. A measure of judgement is not a measure of experience, and neither is it a measure of whether a life contains the goods, such as health, friendship and freedom, that most traditions of thought have held to be worth having whatever one happens to feel about them.

A sensible policy, then, would treat satisfaction scores as one instrument among several, read alongside measures of how people actually spend and feel their days and of what they are really able to do. Used alone, the scores reward whatever lowers expectations as readily as whatever improves lives, and a government that steered by them alone could succeed by teaching its citizens to want less.

passage: For most of the twentieth century, readers of newspapers paid only a fraction of what their papers cost to produce. The rest came from advertisers, who were buying not journalism but attention, and the arrangement was so familiar that few people thought about it. Readers believed that they were buying a newspaper; in commercial terms, they were the product being sold. When advertising money migrated to online platforms that could target audiences more precisely, many news organisations turned to the readers themselves and asked them to subscribe. The change has been widely welcomed, and with some reason. A publication that lives on subscriptions answers to the people who read it rather than to the firms that want to sell them things, and it has less incentive to chase the cheap, fleeting clicks on which online advertising depends.

Yet the subscription model carries a cost that its admirers tend to pass over. Advertising, whatever its faults, made news cheap for the reader and therefore widely shared. A wall that admits only paying readers divides the public into those who can afford careful reporting and those who cannot, or will not, pay for it. The second group does not stop reading. It turns to whatever is free, and what is free is increasingly material that is cheap to produce: opinion, aggregation, rumour and content funded by people with something to promote, whether a product, a cause or a candidate. The result is a two-tier system in which the quality of what one knows depends partly on what one spends.

This matters more for news than for most products because the value of good reporting does not stay with the person who buys it. A voter who is misinformed about a local budget affects the outcome for neighbours who read every line of it, and a neighbourhood in which most residents rely on rumour about a planning dispute will reach worse decisions, which the careful reader who paid for accurate coverage must then live with. In this respect news behaves less like a private purchase and more like public health: the well-informed are not fully protected if those around them are not.

The conclusion to draw is not that news should go back to an advertising model that has largely collapsed, nor that we should pretend that journalism can be given away without someone paying for it. Free news was never really free; its price was simply hidden in the cost of the soap and cars its advertisers sold. The question is how to keep the independence that reader revenue brings while limiting the exclusion it creates. Some answers are familiar: lifting the wall for stories of urgent public importance, cheaper access for students and libraries, and public or philanthropic support for reporting that markets will not fund. None is sufficient alone. But a news system should be judged not only by the quality of its best journalism but by how many people that journalism actually reaches.

passage: Among researchers who study catastrophes, a slogan has become something close to a creed: there is no such thing as a natural disaster. The claim is not that earthquakes, floods and cyclones are human inventions. It is that a hazard, a physical event of a certain size, becomes a disaster only when it meets people and structures unable to withstand it. A cyclone that crosses an empty coastline is a fact about the atmosphere; the same cyclone striking a crowded delta of unreinforced houses with no warning system is a social event, and the scale of its damage is decided as much by the delta's history as by the storm.

The slogan earns its popularity because it redirects attention to what can be changed. Two cities shaken by earthquakes of similar strength may suffer wholly different losses, one counting broken windows and the other thousands of dead, and the difference lies in building standards, in whether they were enforced, in where the poor were permitted or forced to live. Calling the outcome natural lets those decisions disappear from view. It encourages the belief that loss is fate, and fate calls for sympathy after the event rather than investment before it.

Taken literally, however, the slogan claims too much. Some events are large enough that no plausible arrangement of society would have prevented great loss: a sufficiently large eruption, or a wave of extraordinary height arriving within minutes, can overwhelm even well-prepared places. To insist that every such loss was socially produced is to imply that someone could have prevented it, which may be false, and in its cruder versions comes close to suggesting that the people harmed were responsible for their own exposure. The slogan can also tempt its users to neglect the physical science of hazards, as though knowing how often floods of a given size recur mattered less than studying the societies they strike, when the two kinds of knowledge are needed together.

The insight is worth keeping and the absolutism worth dropping. A more defensible claim is that the size of a disaster is never simply natural: the hazard sets the challenge, but how much of the challenge becomes catastrophe depends on choices made long before. This version keeps the slogan's critical edge, its refusal to let preventable deaths be filed under bad luck, while admitting that nature sometimes sets challenges that no society could fully meet.

passage: Most people who hold opinions about celebrated modern buildings have never been inside them. They know them from photographs, and the photographs share a family resemblance. They are taken in the weeks after completion, before the occupants have moved in, on a day chosen for its light. Furniture, if there is any, is placed by the photographer; people, if they appear at all, are small and blurred, present to give scale rather than to show use. The building is caught at the single moment when it most resembles its architect's intention and least resembles the place it will become.

There is nothing sinister in this. The photographer is paid to show the work at its best, as a portrait painter is, and an empty room displays its proportions more clearly than a crowded one. The difficulty lies in what happens when such images become the principal medium through which architecture is judged. Reputations are made in magazines and, increasingly, on screens, and they are made quickly, long before anyone knows whether the roof leaks, whether the offices overheat in summer, or whether the grand atrium is a pleasure to cross on a wet Monday morning. Critics, who seldom have the time or the budget to return, write from the same images, and the first account of a building tends to become the account that is repeated. A building's reputation is thus fixed at the very moment when least is known about it.

The effect is not confined to critics. Architects are not naive about how their work will be seen, and a profession whose rewards follow the photograph will tend, without anyone deciding it, to design for the photograph. Qualities that register in a single frame, a dramatic cantilever, a pure white surface, a striking silhouette against the sky, come to be favoured over qualities that can be experienced only over time or through the other senses: the way a staircase feels under tired feet, the acoustics of a dining room, the dignity with which a material ages. White render photographs beautifully and often weathers badly; a brick that looks dull on the day of opening may look better in its fiftieth year than in its first.

Defenders of the photograph reply that it is the only way most of us can see buildings in distant cities, and that the alternative, judging only what one has personally visited, would make criticism parochial. They add that many buildings which photograph well also work well, and that architects idealised their work in drawings long before the camera existed. Each of these points is fair, yet none of them reaches the central point. The complaint is not that photographs flatter, which drawings did too, but that the moment of photographing has become the moment of judgement, and that the qualities a photograph can register have quietly become the qualities that count.

One modest remedy would be to make the second look as normal as the first. A building photographed and discussed again after ten years of use, with its occupants in it and its materials weathered, would be judged on evidence that the opening day cannot supply. Such a practice would not abolish the glamour of the new, and it is not meant to. It would simply give the slower virtues of a building a chance to be seen by those who will never walk through it, and it would give architects a reason to care about the tenth year as much as the first, since that is when they would next be judged.

passage: Discussions of antibiotic resistance usually begin with misuse: drugs prescribed for viral infections that they cannot touch, courses abandoned halfway, animals dosed to make them grow faster. Each of these practices gives bacteria more opportunities to evolve defences, and each deserves the attention it receives. Less often discussed is a quieter problem that has nothing to do with carelessness. Even if every prescription were perfectly judged, the way new antibiotics are paid for would discourage anyone from making them.

Consider what responsible use of a genuinely new antibiotic would look like. Because every use exerts selective pressure, the new drug should be held back for patients whose infections resist older and cheaper treatments, and it should be prescribed as rarely as possible for as long as possible. This is sound medicine. It is also a commercial disaster. A company recovers the cost of developing a drug by selling it in quantity during the years its patent protects it, and a drug that doctors are urged not to use cannot be sold in quantity. The contrast with a medicine for a chronic condition, taken every day for decades by millions of people, could hardly be sharper. It is not surprising that large firms have drifted out of the field, or that small firms that have brought new antibiotics through approval have sometimes failed commercially soon afterwards.

The proposed remedy is to separate a company's income from the number of doses it sells. Under such schemes, a health system would pay a fixed annual sum for access to a new antibiotic, whether it is used on a thousand patients or on ten, much as a town pays for a fire brigade whether or not anything burns that year. The payment rewards the existence of the drug rather than its consumption, which is exactly the property a reserve antibiotic is supposed to have.

The objections are real. Such payments are large, they must be justified to budget holders who see little use for their money, and nobody knows quite how to price a drug whose value lies mainly in emergencies it may never have to meet. Nor would better payment by itself guarantee discovery, since finding compounds that kill resistant bacteria without harming patients is scientifically hard. But these difficulties argue for designing the schemes carefully, not for abandoning them. The alternative is to go on rewarding a pattern of sales that good medicine forbids, and to discover the cost only when the older drugs have stopped working.

passage: When a market collapses, the verdict arrives quickly: it was a bubble, and those who bought near the top were caught up in a collective madness. The diagnosis is comforting, because it implies that the error was obvious and that sober people would have avoided it. It is also, in a great many cases, a judgement that could have been made only afterwards. A price that later falls by three quarters was not necessarily irrational when it was paid; it may have been a reasonable wager on an outcome that simply did not occur.

Consider the shares of firms built around a genuinely new technology. No one knows at the outset which of them will dominate, how large the market will become, or how long any dominance will last. A high price for the whole group can reflect the small chance of an enormous success for one or two of its members, and when most of them then fail, the collapse in prices is consistent with the original bet having been a sensible one. Hindsight converts uncertainty into folly by forgetting that the winners were not known in advance. The same consideration explains why confident announcements that a bubble is under way have such a mixed record, since prices have sometimes gone on rising for years after the warning was issued.

None of this shows that bubbles are a myth. Something does distinguish a bubble from a failed bet, but it is not the size of the eventual fall; it is the reason for which the asset was bought. A buyer who pays a high price because she believes the asset will yield returns that justify it is making a wager that may be mistaken but is not speculative in the narrow sense. A buyer who pays the price only because he expects someone else to pay more, and who would not hold the asset on its own merits for a day, is taking part in something of a different kind: a chain whose value depends on recruiting a next buyer, and which must at some point break.

The difficulty is that this distinguishing mark lies in motives, and prices do not record motives. Two buyers paying the same price on the same day may be doing quite different things, and an observer who sees only the price cannot tell how much of a market consists of believers and how much of passers-on. That is why proposals that regulators should identify bubbles as they form and deflate them, by raising interest rates or restricting purchases, ask for a judgement that is rarely available in time, and why such measures, if applied, are likely to fall on sound and unsound investments alike.

A more modest aim is within reach. What turns the collapse of a price into a wider calamity is usually not the fall itself but the borrowing that financed the purchases, because losses on borrowed money pass from the buyer to the lender, and from the lender to everyone who depends on it. Limits on leverage do not require anyone to know whether a price is justified; they require only that whoever turns out to be wrong should be wrong mainly with his own money. This is less dramatic than a promise to prick bubbles before they grow, and it will disappoint those who want the next crash prevented rather than contained, but a rule that works without foresight has the considerable merit of not depending on a capacity that no one possesses. Such a policy does not aim to prevent bubbles. It aims to make them survivable.

passage: When readers began, in large numbers, to write and circulate their own stories about the characters of popular novels and television series, the reaction from some authors was indignation. The characters were theirs, they said; to send them on adventures their creators had never imagined, to pair them with new lovers or to bring the dead back to life was a kind of trespass. Defenders of the practice replied with equal heat that a story, once released into the world, belongs to those who love it, and that the fans who keep a fictional world alive with their own inventions have a better claim to it than the person who merely began it. Both sides, I think, have misdescribed what is at stake.

Consider first how unusual the authors' position is, historically speaking. For most of the history of storytelling, retelling was the ordinary way in which stories lived. The same heroes passed from one teller to another, gaining episodes, companions and endings along the way; a poet who took up an old legend was expected to change it, and was admired for the changes. The idea that a fictional person belongs to a single creator, and that others may not set that person in new situations, took shape alongside printing, markets for books and laws that made authorship a form of property. It is not a natural fact about stories, though it now feels like one. Fan writers, from this angle, are less the vandals of a settled order than the late heirs of a much older one.

Yet the fans' champions claim too much when they turn this history into a counter-theory of ownership. To say that a story belongs to those who love it is still to speak of belonging, merely moving the title deeds from one party to another. What the older practice suggests is rather that stories are not the sort of thing that is owned in the first place, though particular tellings are. An author can reasonably object to having her text copied and sold under someone else's name, or to having her own work altered and passed off as hers. It is much harder to see what she loses when a reader imagines her characters on another afternoon, so long as no one mistakes that afternoon for one she wrote. The distinction between a text and a world is precisely the one that both sides have blurred.

There is an irony here that deserves notice. Fan communities, which began by contesting an author's exclusive authority, have often developed authorities of their own. Long debates arise over what counts as 'canon', over which inventions are faithful and which are betrayals, and newcomers who ignore the accumulated rules can be treated with a severity that few authors would dare to show their readers. In such moments the community reproduces, on a smaller scale, the very proprietary attitude it set out to resist, as though the impulse to fix a story and guard its boundaries were not peculiar to authors but a temptation that comes with loving any story at all.

None of this settles every case, and there are surely retellings that wound in ways the distinction does not capture, as when a living author's characters are put to uses she finds degrading. But it does suggest a more useful question than the one with which the quarrel began, which asked whose story it is. The better question is what each kind of claim protects: the integrity of a particular telling, which deserves defence, or the boundaries of an imagined world, which, on the evidence of the long history of storytelling, have never been defensible for long.

passage: Few doctrines have been more often misunderstood by sympathetic outsiders than the Buddhist teaching of anatta, usually translated as 'no-self'. Stated baldly, as the claim that there is no self, it seems to invite an easy refutation: someone, after all, is entertaining the doctrine, and someone will be disappointed if it turns out to be false. Critics who press this point imagine that they have found a contradiction at the heart of the tradition. In fact they have mostly found a problem of translation, and behind it a mistaken assumption about what kind of claim the teaching was meant to be.

In the early discourses the teaching typically appears not as a thesis about what exists but as an exercise. The listener is led through the components that make up a person, which the tradition groups as bodily form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, and is asked of each whether it is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it is under one's control. Since none of them passes these tests, none, the discourse concludes, should be regarded as 'mine', as what 'I am', or as 'my self'. The point of the exercise is practical. According to the tradition's own account of suffering, its origin lies in craving, and craving is sustained by the habit of treating changing and uncontrollable processes as possessions one must defend. To see that nothing in experience is fit to be owned in that way is to loosen the grip of the habit.

Read in this light, the easy refutation misses its target. The teaching does not deny that there is a stream of experiences, nor that the stream has a history, makes choices and bears their consequences; the same tradition has a great deal to say about all three. What it denies is that there is, in addition to the stream, an unchanging owner standing behind it, and it denies this chiefly because belief in such an owner is what makes us cling. A later dialogue makes the point with a chariot: the word names an assembly of axle, wheels and frame, and nothing is lost by admitting that there is no further chariot over and above the parts, arranged as they are. The person, likewise, is a convenient name for a functioning whole, not a hidden thing to which the whole belongs.

It would be too convenient, however, to conclude that the doctrine is purely therapeutic and therefore immune to philosophical scrutiny. A therapy that works by inducing a belief earns its authority only if the belief is warranted; otherwise it is a comforting fiction, and the tradition has never presented its teaching as a fiction. The exercise succeeds, by its own standards, because it reveals how things are. So the metaphysical question cannot be set aside; it can only be stated more precisely. The question is not whether anyone exists but whether a person is anything more than the organised stream, and on that question the doctrine takes a position that some philosophers in other traditions have also defended, and others have rejected, without anyone having settled the matter.

The lesson for the sympathetic outsider is therefore double. The easy refutation fails, because it attacks a claim the teaching does not make. But the easy defence fails too, because the teaching is not merely a technique; it is a technique whose authority rests on a claim about the self that may be true or false, and that deserves to be argued about on its merits rather than admired from a respectful distance.

passage: Few health instructions are repeated as confidently as the one about sleep: adults need about eight hours, and those hours should come in a single unbroken block. Someone who wakes at three in the morning and lies awake for an hour is likely to describe the experience as a disorder, and to spend the next day worrying about it. Advice is sought, remedies are bought, and an hour of wakefulness becomes a problem to be solved. Yet the second half of that instruction, the part about continuity, has a shorter history than its confidence suggests.

Historians reading diaries, legal testimony and household advice from pre-industrial Europe have noticed casual references to a 'first sleep' and a 'second sleep', separated by a spell of wakefulness in the middle of the night. People used that interval to pray, tend the fire, talk quietly, or simply lie in the dark and think. What is striking about these references is not their content but their tone: the waking interval is mentioned as an ordinary feature of the night, not as a complaint. One explanation offered for its later disappearance is the spread of cheap artificial light, which pushed bedtimes later and compressed the night into a single shorter stretch, though the evidence for this is suggestive rather than conclusive.

If consolidated sleep is partly a product of custom, then some of what is now labelled insomnia may be a mismatch between a person and a norm rather than a fault in the person. This matters because worry about sleep is itself a powerful disrupter of sleep. A person who wakes in the night and concludes that something has gone wrong becomes more alert, and stays awake longer, than one who regards the waking as unremarkable. The norm, in other words, can help produce the very failures it is used to diagnose.

It would be a mistake, however, to replace one myth with another. The historical record does not show that segmented sleep is the true human pattern from which industrial society has led us astray; it shows that sleep has taken more than one form, depending on light, work and season. Nor does any of this make chronic sleep loss harmless. People who sleep too little over long periods do suffer for it, and some sleep complaints call for medical attention. The modest lesson is that a description of how many people sleep should not be mistaken for a rule about how everyone must.

passage: Few kinds of article travel as easily as the list of untranslatable words. A language is said to possess a single word for the particular light that falls through leaves, another for the guilty pleasure of buying books one will never read, a third for the melancholy of a Sunday evening, and the reader is invited to marvel that English, or whatever language the list happens to be written in, has nothing to match them. The lists are charming, and most of the words in them are real. What is doubtful is the conclusion they are usually taken to support: that the speakers of a language without such a word cannot quite have the experience it names, or that a vocabulary is a window onto a national soul.

Look at what the lists actually demonstrate. Each entry pairs a foreign word with a sentence or two of English explaining it, and the explanation is usually clear enough that the reader recognises the experience at once, often with a small shock of familiarity. The list, in other words, translates every word it calls untranslatable. What it shows is not that a meaning cannot cross from one language to another but that one language packages in a single word what another expresses in a phrase. That is a fact about how vocabularies happen to be divided up, and it tells us very little about what their speakers are able to think or feel. Every language lacks single words for countless things its speakers understand perfectly well.

This is not to say that nothing is lost when such a word is carried across. A single word is easy to reach for; a phrase is not. A word that ordinary speakers use daily carries the weight of all those uses, along with a register, a sound and a set of associations that no paraphrase reproduces. The very existence of the word suggests that a community has found the experience worth naming, and that fact is itself a small piece of cultural information. For a translator working on a poem, where sound and compression matter as much as sense, these losses are real and constant, and no amount of explanation in a footnote restores them.

But the losses are of degree, not of kind, and they are not peculiar to exotic words. They occur whenever any word is rendered by another, and even within a single language, where no two synonyms carry quite the same associations. Seen this way, the romance of the untranslatable flatters everyone involved: the reader, who feels worldly for knowing the rare word, and a picture of cultures as sealed rooms whose inhabitants can only be gazed at, never understood. The more modest and more accurate lesson is that translation is always possible and never complete, and that its difficulties lie less in the dictionary than in everything a word drags along with it.

passage: The word 'stress' entered the study of living things from the study of materials, where its meaning is reasonably exact: the internal force per unit area within a body subjected to a load. In engineering, stress is distinguished from strain, the deformation that the load produces, and both are distinguished from the load itself. When the word was borrowed to describe what happens to organisms under pressure, these distinctions did not travel with it. In ordinary speech, and in a good deal of research, 'stress' can refer to the demanding situation, to the bodily and emotional reaction it provokes, or to the relation between the two, and it is often far from clear which of these is meant. A survey announcing that most workers feel stressed may be measuring their workloads, their symptoms or their sense of being overwhelmed, and the headline rarely says which.

The slippage is not merely a matter of untidy usage. Consider the familiar claim that stress is bad for health. If stress means the reaction, and the reaction is defined partly by its harmful effects, the claim is close to true by definition. If stress means the demanding situation, the claim is plainly false as a generalisation, since many people meet heavy demands without harm and some appear to thrive on them. Only if stress means a particular relation, demands that exceed what a person believes they can manage, does the claim become a substantive hypothesis that could turn out to be wrong. Much popular discussion moves among these meanings without noticing, and so acquires the authority of the first reading and the scope of the second.

The same confusion shadows the more recent enthusiasm for 'good stress'. To say that some stress is beneficial may mean that some demanding situations are worth seeking out, which is uncontroversial; or that some physiological reactions to demand improve performance, which is plausible within limits; or that people who interpret their reactions as helpful fare better than those who do not, which is a specific claim requiring specific evidence. Advice built on the phrase often slides from the first meaning, which everyone accepts, to the third, which is the one actually being sold. Each of the three deserves to be judged on its own evidence, and the plausibility of the first lends nothing to the third.

It might seem that the remedy is to abandon the word altogether. That would be a mistake, and not only because ordinary language is not so easily reformed. The very breadth of the term has allowed researchers in physiology, psychology, sociology and medicine to recognise that they were studying related things, and it has drawn attention to connections, between working conditions and heart disease, say, that narrower vocabularies might have kept apart. Whole programmes of research, on bereavement, on unemployment, on the burdens of caring for a sick relative, found a common frame in it. A concept can be scientifically fruitful precisely because it is loose at the edges, so long as those who use it know where the looseness lies.

What the word cannot do is carry an argument by itself. The useful discipline is to ask, whenever a claim about stress is made, which of its meanings is in play, and whether the evidence offered supports the claim under that meaning or only under a different one. A finding about reactions does not automatically license advice about situations, and a finding about interpretations says little about either. Keeping the senses apart costs a few extra words; failing to keep them apart has cost a good deal of confusion, some of it in the very places where clarity matters most.

passage: Generations of students have learned that science proceeds by a method, and that the method has steps. One observes, forms a hypothesis, designs an experiment, tests the hypothesis and draws a conclusion, after which the cycle begins again. The sequence is tidy, easy to examine and, as a description of what scientists actually do, very nearly useless. It is not that no scientist has ever followed it. It is that the sciences differ so widely in what they are able to do that any single recipe either excludes much of their work or becomes so general that it no longer guides anyone.

Consider the range. An astronomer studying a distant star cannot intervene in it; she can only watch, and her ingenuity lies in finding natural cases that differ in just the respect she wants to compare. A geologist reconstructing how a mountain range formed is not testing a hypothesis by experiment but assembling a history from traces, much as a detective does, and her standard of success is the coherence of a narrative that accounts for scattered evidence. A laboratory chemist may indeed run controlled experiments, but she spends much of her time on something the textbook sequence ignores entirely: making instruments and procedures work at all. To call all of this 'the scientific method' is to give one name to several distinct crafts.

The tidy sequence is not merely inaccurate; it does some damage. By making the controlled experiment the model of all good science, it encourages the view that sciences which cannot experiment are somehow lesser, as though reconstructing the history of the Earth were a provisional activity awaiting a proper laboratory. And by presenting science as a machine that turns hypotheses into conclusions, it leaves the public poorly prepared for the ordinary untidiness of research, in which results conflict, estimates are revised and experts disagree for long periods before they converge. People taught to expect the machine are apt to read each revision as a malfunction.

Is there, then, nothing that the sciences share? There is something, but it is not a procedure. What unites the astronomer, the geologist and the chemist is a set of habits about how claims are treated once they have been made: they are exposed to colleagues who are expected to attack them, they are stated in a form that evidence could tell against, and the people who make them are expected to give them up when such evidence arrives. These are norms of a community rather than steps for an individual, and that is precisely why they cannot be captured in a flowchart. A student who had absorbed them would understand science better than one who had memorised the steps, even if she could not say in what order they come.

passage: A library catalogue looks like the least ideological of documents. Its function, apparently, is merely to inform a reader where a particular book is located, and the call number on a spine seems as neutral as a street address. But a classification scheme does more than locate. To place a book, it must first decide what the book is about, and to do that it must divide the whole of knowledge into classes, arrange the classes in an order, and decide which subjects deserve broad territory and which can be squeezed into a corner. Every call number is, in compressed form, a small theory of what its book is about. These are not merely technical decisions. They are judgments about how the world is organised, made by particular people at a particular time, and then built, quite literally, into buildings.

The judgments show most clearly where a scheme meets subjects its makers did not think central. One widely used decimal scheme, devised in the nineteenth century, gave most of the numbers in its religion class to varieties of Christianity, leaving the rest of the world's traditions to share a small remainder. Nobody needs to suppose malice to explain this; the scheme reflected the collections and the assumptions of the libraries its maker knew. But the consequence outlived the assumptions. A library using such a scheme in a city of many faiths must either cram large collections into long, unwieldy numbers or improvise local fixes that make its shelves harder to share with other libraries.

The effect is not confined to how much space a subject receives. Classification also governs adjacency, and adjacency governs discovery. A reader who goes to the shelf for one book finds its neighbours, and much of what people learn in libraries they learn through this kind of sideways encounter. Suppose a hypothetical study of household labour is shelved among works on economics; its browsers will meet it as an argument about production and value. Shelved instead among works on the family, it will be met as an argument about domestic life. The book is the same, but the conversation it is placed in is not, and the scheme, rather than the author, has chosen the conversation.

From this one might conclude that classification is a kind of censorship which libraries should abandon in favour of keyword search, which appears to impose no order at all. The conclusion does not follow. Search systems rank their results, and ranking embodies choices just as surely as shelving does; the choices are merely harder to see. Moreover, a collection with no arrangement is not neutral but unusable, since a reader can then find only what she already knows to ask for, whereas the browser of a well-ordered shelf may stumble on books she never knew existed. Some order is the price of a library's being useful, and every order has a point of view.

The more defensible lesson is that classification should be treated as revisable and should be visible as a choice. What can reasonably be asked of one is that it knows it is not, and that it leaves room for readers to cross the boundaries it draws.

passage: Architects tend to speak of a building as finished on the day it is handed over, and most architectural criticism shares the assumption. For its occupants, however, the handover is a beginning. Within a few years the first partitions have gone up or come down, a porch has been enclosed, a garage has become a bedroom, and the building has started to diverge from its drawings. A family grows and then shrinks, a business expands into the floor above, a school changes the way it teaches, and each of these shifts leaves its mark on the fabric. Over a century the divergence can be so complete that little of the original arrangement survives except the outer walls and the structural frame. If we want to know how well a building has been designed, the question of how it absorbs such changes deserves at least as much attention as the question of how it looked when new.

The obvious response is to design for change, and for several decades architects attempted exactly that. Offices and schools were built as open floors with movable partitions, and houses with walls that could slide, fold or be unbolted, so that occupants could rearrange the interior at will. The results were often disappointing. Movable partitions were seldom moved, because moving them was laborious and disturbed the services concealed within them; the flexible plan turned out to be a plan that suited no particular use well; and the occupants, rather than enjoying their freedom, filled the space with improvised screens and cabinets to make the rooms that the design had declined to provide. Designing for every possible use, it emerged, had been a way of designing for none.

The buildings that have in fact proved most adaptable are frequently ones that were never designed with change in mind. Old warehouses and mills, with their regular grids of columns, generous ceiling heights and thick, plain walls, have been turned into flats, studios, schools and offices with surprising ease. Terraced houses built for one family have been divided into apartments and, a generation later, joined up again. What these buildings share is not flexibility in the engineered sense but a kind of slack: dimensions a little larger than any one use required, a structure simple enough to be understood by ordinary builders, and surfaces that can be cut into without catastrophe. The ordinary builder called in to knock two rooms together can see at once where the loads run and what may safely be taken away. They fit their first use loosely, and that looseness is what lets them fit their later uses at all.

The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a profession that prides itself on precision. A building tailored exactly to its brief, every room sized to its programme and every service routed to suit it, is admirable on the day of opening and brittle thereafter, because the brief will change and the building cannot. Generosity of this kind costs something at the outset, in floor area and in height, and clients are seldom eager to pay for space that nobody has yet asked for. This is not an argument against all precision; an operating theatre or a laboratory must fit its use closely, and a little slack in the wrong place is merely waste. But for most ordinary buildings, which will outlive the purposes for which they were commissioned, the more durable virtue is a certain generosity, together with a willingness on the architect's part to regard the occupants' later alterations not as defacement but as the building continuing to do its job.

passage: Ask a collector why she keeps buying stamps, coins or toy cars long after there is any room left to display them, and the answer is rarely about the objects themselves. More often it concerns a gap: the one issue missing from a run, the single variant that would finish a set. Collecting, on this view, is less a love of things than a love of completion. The individual stamp matters because of the place it occupies in a series, and its value to the collector rises sharply as the series nears its end, often far beyond anything a buyer outside the hobby would think of paying.

Manufacturers learned long ago to exploit this. A cereal box that contains one of twelve plastic figures, a sticker album with a few deliberately scarce pages, a line of trading cards issued in waves: each turns an ordinary purchase into a step towards a whole that the buyer did not know he wanted until he was shown its outline. The empty album is the real product. Once its spaces are printed, every blank becomes a small reproach, and the purchase that fills it brings a satisfaction out of all proportion to what was bought.

It would be easy to conclude that collecting is simply a manufactured compulsion, a weakness that the market has learned to farm. That conclusion goes too far. Many of the most devoted collectors pursue series that no company ever designed: the railway timetables of a vanished line, the matchboxes of hotels that have since closed, the scattered editions of a minor poet. Here it is the collector who defines the set, deciding what counts as belonging to it and therefore what counts as missing. Such collecting is a way of ordering the world, of drawing a boundary around a scattered field and making it intelligible. Many museums began, in part, as exactly this kind of private project.

The difference between the two kinds of collecting is not the passion involved, which can be equally intense, but who holds the map. When the series is invented by a seller, completion is a target set by someone else, and the finish line is often moved just as it comes into view, with a new wave or a special edition. When the collector draws the map, completion is a judgement she makes for herself, and the pleasure lies as much in the defining as in the finding. The danger of the commercial version is not that it creates desire, since all collecting does that, but that it quietly takes the act of definition away from the person doing the collecting.

passage: We tend to think of the passport as a document that lets people travel. It is the thing we pack and check twice before leaving for the airport, and losing it abroad feels like being stranded. Yet the history of the passport suggests that its first purpose was not to open borders but to give states a means of closing them selectively. A document that certifies who you are, and which state answers for you, is above all a tool for deciding who may enter, who may leave, and who may be turned back.

For much of the nineteenth century, a traveller could cross many European frontiers without being asked for papers at all. Controls existed, but they were patchy, and in several countries they were relaxed as railways made movement faster and cheaper. The First World War changed this. Governments anxious about spies, deserters and the flight of men of fighting age began demanding documents at every crossing, and when the war ended the requirement was not withdrawn. What had been introduced as an emergency measure became the ordinary condition of international travel, and the expectation that every person should belong to exactly one state, and carry proof of it, hardened into common sense. Few people now remember that it was ever otherwise.

None of this makes the passport simply an instrument of control. For the person who holds it, it is also a claim on protection: it entitles the bearer to return home and to seek help from the officials of the issuing state when abroad. The predicament of stateless people, who have no government willing to vouch for them, shows how much that claim is worth. Without it, a person can be refused entry everywhere and expelled from wherever he happens to be.

The more uncomfortable point is that the protection is unevenly distributed. Two travellers standing in the same queue may carry documents of identical design and very different power, one admitting its holder to most of the world without a visa, the other inviting suspicion at every desk. What the passport records, then, is not only identity but rank in an order of states, an accident of birth that the individual did little to earn and can rarely change. Nor is that rank settled by anything the traveller does at the desk; it is negotiated between governments, through visa agreements and reciprocal arrangements, long before any individual reaches the frontier. To call the document a passport to freedom is to describe the experience of those whose papers happen to work.

passage: Debates about the informal economy, the vast realm of unregistered firms and unprotected work that employs a majority of workers in many poorer countries, tend to divide into two camps. One sees informality as exclusion. On this account, people sell vegetables on pavements or take casual work on building sites because the formal economy has too few jobs to absorb them; informality is a waiting room, and its occupants would leave if a door opened. The other camp sees informality as a choice. Registering a business, paying taxes and complying with labour law are costly, and for many firms the benefits of formality, such as access to the courts and to bank credit, are not worth the price. Informality, on this account, is a rational response to a state that asks much and offers little.

Each camp marshals real evidence, and each tends to generalise from the cases that suit it. The exclusion view draws on the lives of the poorest informal workers, whose earnings are low, whose hours are long and who report that they would gladly take a salaried job. The choice view draws on a different population: owners of small but established workshops and trading firms who could register, who know what registration would involve and who have decided against it. Both groups are informal. They are not otherwise much alike, and an argument about which of them represents the informal economy is rather like an argument about whether the typical resident of a city is a banker or a street sweeper.

The distinction matters most when governments decide to act. Programmes that cut the cost of registration, by reducing fees, merging permits or allowing firms to register online, are well designed for the second group and largely irrelevant to the first. A woman frying snacks at a bus stand is not informal because the registration form is long; she is informal because what she earns would not cover the obligations that formality brings, and because no employer has offered her anything better. For her, simplification changes nothing. Campaigns that instead treat informality as evasion and respond with fines and evictions fall hardest on precisely those who had the least choice.

It would be wrong to conclude that the informal economy is merely a collection of unrelated cases. The groups are linked, since established informal firms often employ, supply or buy from the poorest workers, and conditions in one tier affect the other. But the links are a reason to design policy for each tier with the others in view, not a reason to pretend that one diagnosis fits all. The question to ask about any informal worker is not whether informality is chosen or imposed in general, but which of the two it is for that worker.

passage: The phrase 'conspicuous consumption', coined by Thorstein Veblen in the 1890s, named a habit of the wealthy of his day: the purchase of goods whose chief use was to show that one could afford them. The mansion, the carriage and the idle household were, on this account, less comforts than advertisements. The idea proved so useful that it outlived the society that prompted it, and it still shapes how we picture status spending: the logo on the handbag, the oversized car, the watch that costs more than a year's rent.

The picture now misleads more than it reveals, at least at the top. As mass production and global supply chains have made once-rare goods cheap, the handbag and the car have become available, in passable imitations, to almost anyone with a credit card. Display of this kind has lost much of its power to separate, and many of the most advantaged households have turned away from it. Their spending flows instead into things that are hard to see and harder to copy: private tuition and a house in the right school catchment, retirement savings, organic groceries, exercise classes, domestic help that frees time for reading, and clothing whose quality is recognised only by those who know what to look for. The signal, where there is one, is addressed to a narrow audience of peers rather than to the street. Call this inconspicuous consumption.

It would be easy to treat the change as an improvement in taste, a retreat from vulgar display into quieter and more sensible habits. In part it is. Much of this spending yields real benefits in health, in learning and in security, and few would wish the rich to return to buying gold-plated taps. But the shift has two consequences that the language of good taste conceals. The first is that inconspicuous goods are more effective at reproducing advantage than conspicuous ones ever were. A diamond can be sold; a childhood spent in good schools, with books at home and parents who have time, becomes part of a person and can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later. Spending of this kind does not merely display a position; it passes it on.

The second consequence is moral. Conspicuous consumption invited criticism precisely because it was conspicuous. The flashy car was an obvious target for the satirist and the moralist, and its owner could be accused of vanity. Inconspicuous consumption is much harder to criticise, because it presents itself not as display but as virtue: one is not showing off, one is merely eating well, looking after one's health and investing in one's children. The vocabulary that surrounds it, of wellness, sensible choices and doing the best for one's family, offers the satirist nothing obviously vulgar to mock. Those who cannot afford to do the same are not envied so much as quietly judged, as though their diets and their children's results were failures of character rather than of income.

None of this is an accusation of bad faith. It does not require us to think the affluent hypocritical, or the parent paying for tuition secretly bent on buying status; most such choices are made sincerely, for the reasons people give. The point is structural rather than personal. A society in which advantage is transmitted through the visible accumulation of objects at least makes its inequalities legible. One in which advantage flows through habits, schooling and time has made them harder to see, and inequalities that are hard to see are also harder to argue about.

passage: Few findings in social psychology have escaped the laboratory as completely as the bystander effect. In its popular form it says that the more people witness an emergency, the less likely the victim is to receive help, and it is usually offered as evidence of modern apathy: crowds of onlookers, each waiting for someone else to act. The idea owes much of its fame to a newspaper account of a murder in a city street in the 1960s, in which dozens of neighbours were said to have watched and done nothing. Later investigation suggested that the account greatly exaggerated both the number of witnesses and their indifference, but by then the story had become a parable.

The experiments that followed were more careful than the parable. Their central claim was not that people are callous but that responsibility, when shared, is diluted. A person who believes that she alone has heard a cry for help knows that if she does not act, no one will; a person who knows that others have heard it can reasonably suppose that someone better placed is already responding. Ambiguity compounds the effect. In a group, each witness looks to the others to work out whether anything is really wrong, and the calm faces of people who are themselves only watching can persuade everyone that nothing is.

Yet there is a gap between what these studies measured and what the popular version claims. They showed that a given individual is less likely to help when others are present. They did not show that a victim is less likely to be helped. The two come apart because a crowd contains many potential helpers: even if each one is somewhat less willing, the chance that at least one of them steps forward can remain high, and may rise as the crowd grows. Some recent studies of recorded conflicts in public places have reported that in most of them at least one bystander intervened, a pattern hard to reconcile with the image of the paralysed crowd.

None of this makes the original research worthless. The mechanisms it identified are real, and they help explain why emergencies in which no one is sure what is happening, or whose job it is to act, can go unanswered. What it does not support is a sweeping verdict on human nature. The practical advice that follows from the research is modest and useful: if you need help, single out one person and tell that person what to do, so that responsibility is no longer shared and the situation is no longer ambiguous.
